title: Avista Management, Inc. v. Wausau Underwriters Insurance Co.
lead: Counsel cannot agree on a deposition location, so the judge prescribes a single game to choose within fixed geographic and scheduling limits, with review reserved to him.

actors.name: Avista Management, Inc., doing business as Avista Plex
actors.role: Plaintiff asking the court to designate the deposition location.

actors.name: Judge Gregory A. Presnell
actors.role: District judge issuing the limited logistical order.

proceedings: Avista filed document 105 seeking a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition location.
Presnell denied that motion and prescribed a selection procedure with a possible review hearing.
limits: The order does not describe underlying insurance merits or establish that the game occurred. The courthouse site was conditional, and the stated appeal was review before the issuing district judge. No general rule authorizing chance-based merits adjudication was announced.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A deposition-location disagreement reaches the judge
sections.cue: What question did Avista ask the court to decide?
paragraphs: Avista Management, doing business as Avista Plex, was litigating against Wausau Underwriters Insurance Company in the Middle District of Florida. Avista filed document 105 asking the court to designate the location for a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition.

District Judge Gregory A. Presnell described the disagreement as another matter counsel had failed to untangle without federal-court help. His June 6, 2006 order denied the location-designation motion. It did not describe the underlying insurance claims, identify competing preferred locations or adjudicate substantive liability.

sections.title: The order sets a single game and a conditional meeting place
sections.cue: What would the lawyers do on June 30?
paragraphs: Rather than choose the deposition site himself, Presnell directed counsel to resolve that limited question through one game of rock, paper, scissors. They were to meet at 4 p.m. on June 30, 2006 at a mutually acceptable neutral location. Only if they could not agree on that meeting place would they use the front steps of the Sam M. Gibbons United States Courthouse in Tampa.

Each lawyer could bring one paralegal as attendant and witness. The winner could choose the deposition location, but it had to be in Hillsborough County. These directions concerned selection of a site, not the merits of the lawsuit.

sources.pinpoint: Game, location fallback and selection limit; order 1–2

sections.title: Judicial review and the deposition window remain fixed
sections.cue: What events did the order schedule without reporting their occurrence?
paragraphs: Either party could challenge the game’s outcome. The order called that an appeal and scheduled a July 7, 2006 hearing at 8:30 a.m. before Presnell in Orlando. It meant review by the issuing district judge, not an appeal described as going to a circuit court. The deposition itself was to occur during July 11–12, 2006.

The two-page instrument does not say counsel actually played, identify a winner or report a request for review. It supplied no broader legal test or cited authority for using games. Its limited case-management command preserved timing, location and judicial-review constraints, with no separate writing or footnote.

sources.pinpoint: Review, deposition schedule and scope; order 1–2
